findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, in plain words. That covers the 'what' and 'why' before any jargon appears.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The page links straight from the top to concrete next steps: prerequisites, git clone, ./setup.sh, then `athena ask "add a changelog"`. A newcomer knows what to do next without reading the rest of the page.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" (header) and the Next steps section

findings.text: Firstmate is mentioned here before the page says what it is; the definition only comes under 'Start here'. For a moment the newcomer may not know why this page is about a different project.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project..."

findings.text: This link sits in the header and is meant for the owner, not a visitor. A newcomer may think it is meant for them, or wonder what 'proposals' are.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: Most of the page is a detailed state machine of firstmate's internals with claim ids on every line. That is good evidence that Athena can trace its statements, but it is heavy going for a newcomer, and the page never says this part can be skipped.
Some terms are never properly explained: 'wake', 'endpoint' and 'captain-held inventory' are not defined. 'Stale wake' is defined using the word 'wake' itself.
findings.source: "stale wake: A wake after which the agent inspects a worker..."; "its captain-held inventory is verified"

findings.text: Athena's main promise is a traceable commit with its cost, but the page shows no example of one. It also gives no idea what a run costs. The study shows Athena reading a project, not making a change.
findings.source: "get back a commit they can trace to the request, the models, the cost and the verdict"

findings.text: The prerequisites are specific, which helps. But the page does not say whether a Rust toolchain or a model account or API key is needed, so a newcomer may hit a surprise during setup.
findings.source: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm"

findings.text: The page says openly that it ran nothing and leaves unanswered what it could not find, such as what counts as 'in scope'. That makes it easier to trust.
findings.source: Limits of this study: "This study read the pinned tree only... no failure or retry edge was observed"

findings.text: This points to a folder in the repository without a link. A newcomer on the website cannot follow it.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data"
